title: Verbs that don't care about time
goal: Use *mag-* verbs in three stages — done, ongoing, coming — and see that Tagalog marks stages, not tense.

notes: **Tagalog has no tense — it has stages.** The verb doesn't ask "when?" but "has it started, has it finished?" So *nagluto* covers anything already done — yesterday, this morning, or five years ago. The *when* comes from time words (*kahapon*, *kanina*, *noong isang taon*), not from the verb.

**Mag- turns into nag- once the action has started.** This is the key to the whole system: an *m-* prefix means not started, an *n-* prefix means started. *Magluto* (will/not yet) → *nagluto* (done). The same rule turns *ma-* into *na-* in the next unit.

**Repeating the first syllable means not finished.** *Nagluluto* (is cooking) and *magluluto* (will cook) both repeat *lu-*. The only difference is the first letter: *n-* means started (so: ongoing), *m-* means not started (so: coming).
**The verb comes first.** *Nagluluto ako ng adobo*, not *Ako nagluluto*. The standard order: verb → doer → object → extras. This is the reverse of English and takes a few days of conscious practice.

**The doer is marked with ang or si; the object with ng.** *Nagluluto **ako** ng **adobo*** — the doer is in the spotlight (*ako*, the *ang* set), the object is not (*ng adobo*). This is called actor focus, and unit 13 shows what happens when the spotlight moves.

**Niluluto and ginagawa** in the dialogue use object focus — the form you'll properly meet in unit 13. For now just learn these two whole sentences as everyday questions: *Ano ang niluluto mo?* and *Ano ang ginagawa mo?*
**Hindi pa means "not yet"**, not "no". Answering just *hindi* to *Nag-aral ka ba?* means "no, and I won't". Adding *pa* turns it into "not yet" — almost always more honest and more polite.
**Eh at the end of a sentence** is a softening particle typical of Filipino speech, a bit like "you know" or "though": *Tamad ako eh.* It gives a reason and asks for understanding at the same time.
**Talaga means "really"** and works on its own as a reaction: *Talaga?* — "Really?" One of the words you'll hear most in everyday conversation.

grammars.title: The three stages of mag- verbs
body: Take the root and do two things: choose the prefix (*mag-* if not started, *nag-* if started), and repeat the first syllable of the root if the action isn't finished.
after: **What repeats is the root's first syllable, not the prefix.** *Nagluluto*, not *nanagluto*. Only the first consonant + vowel repeats: *lu-*, *tra-*, *a-*, *li-*.
Roots starting with a vowel take a hyphen after *mag-*: *mag-aral*, *mag-ingat*, *mag-alala*. This is a spelling rule, not a sound.
The two forms beginners mix up most are *nagluluto* (ongoing) and *magluluto* (coming). Only the first letter differs. When in doubt, remember: **n = already rolling, m = not rolling yet.**

grammars.title: Word order in verb sentences
body: Standard Tagalog puts the verb first. Everything else follows in a fairly loose order.
after: Look at the last two rows: as soon as *hindi* appears, the short pronoun jumps in front of the verb. *Hindi ako nag-aral*, not *hindi nag-aral ako*. The same goes for all particles: they gather right after the first word.
To ask who is doing something: *Sino ang nagluluto?* The answer puts the doer up front with *ang*: *Si Mia ang nagluluto.* This *X ang Y* pattern adds emphasis — "it's Mia who's cooking".
To ask what someone is doing: *Ano ang ginagawa mo?* Learn it whole; its cousin *Anong ginagawa mo?* means the same.

blocks.text: *Mag-* verbs tend to mark actions that are **deliberate and carried out by the doer**. This will matter in the next unit, when you meet *-um-* — a verb group covering nearby but not identical ground.

blocks.title: Mag- + English words
items: This prefix is very productive and happily takes English words: *mag-shopping*, *nag-jogging*, *mag-online*, *nag-text*, *mag-Zoom*.
The aspect forms follow the same rules: *nag-shoshopping* (is shopping), *mag-tetext ako* (I'll text). Odd on the page, perfectly normal to the ear.

sections.title: Time words that go with each aspect

blocks.text: Since the verb doesn't mark time, time words do the work. These pairings are the most common.

head: Aspect
Matching time words
Example
rows: bukas, mamaya, sa Lunes, sa susunod

blocks.text: The fourth row deserves attention: **the "ongoing" form is also used for habits.** *Nagtatrabaho ako araw-araw* doesn't mean "I am working every day" but "I work every day". English splits these into two forms; Tagalog uses one.
